sentences: Credit utilization is the most important driver of default risk, accounting for about 28% of the model's importance, and risk increases as utilization rises.

The number of past delinquencies is the second most important driver, accounting for about 17% of importance, and default risk rises with it, with a jump between zero and one or more past delinquencies.
The effect of credit utilization grows with the number of past delinquencies: utilization matters far more for applicants who have past delinquencies than for those who have none.
Income and length of credit history each have a moderate effect, with default risk decreasing as income and credit history length rise.
The debt-to-income ratio has a weak to moderate effect, accounting for about 5% of importance, and default risk increases with it.
Recent credit inquiries have at most a weak effect, while the number of dependents, months at the current address and age hardly matter for default risk.
The data do not settle whether the effects of credit utilization and credit history length interact, though the model shows no clear interaction between them at this sample size.
